'''Edward Thomas Hall''', [[Order of the British Empire|CBE]], [[Fellow of the British Academy|Hon. FBA]], [[Society of Antiquaries of London|FSA]] (10 May 1924 – 11 August 2001), also known as '''Teddy Hall''', was a British scientist and balloonist who is best remembered for exposing the [[Piltdown Man]] as a fraud.

==Early life and education==
Hall was born on 10 May 1924 in [[London]], England, to [[Walter D'Arcy Hall]] and Anne Madeleine Hall.<ref name="WWW" /><ref name="Obit Ind" /> He was brought up at Shipton Court, a [[Jacobean architecture|Jacobean]] manor house in [[Shipton-under-Wychwood]], Oxfordshire.<ref name="Obit Ind" /> He was educated at [[Eton College]], an all-boys [[Public school (United Kingdom)|public school]] in Berkshire. In 1943, he joined the [[Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve]] (RNVR) as an ordinary seaman, serving in landing craft transporting commandos to France.<ref name=":0">{{Citation|last=Pollard|first=A. Mark|title=Hall, Edward T |date=2014|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-0465-2_347|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Global Archaeology|pages=3189–3191|editor-last=Smith|editor-first=Claire|place=New York, NY|publisher=Springer|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-0465-2_347|isbn=978-1-4419-0465-2|access-date=2022-01-04|url-access=subscription}}</ref> 

After the end of the [[Second World War]], he entered [[New College, Oxford]] to study chemistry, and graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] (BA) degree in 1948.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="WWW">{{cite web |title=Hall, Prof. Edward Thomas, (10 May 1924–11 Aug. 2001), Professor, Research Laboratory for Archaeology and the History of Art, Oxford University, 1975–89, then Emeritus Professor of Archaeological Sciences (Director 1954–89); Fellow of Worcester College, Oxford, 1969–89, then Emeritus |url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U18621 |website=[[Who Was Who]] |publisher=Oxford University Press |access-date=15 May 2023 |language=en |date=1 December 2007}}</ref> His [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (DPhil) degree was undertaken at the [[Clarendon Laboratory]] (part of the [[Department of Physics, University of Oxford|Department of Physics]]) under the [[doctoral supervisor|supervision]] of [[Frederick Lindemann, 1st Viscount Cherwell|Lord Cherwell]], and his degree was completed in 1953.<ref name="RLAHA" /><ref name="Obit Ind">{{cite news |last1=Hedges |first1=Robert |last2=Tite |first2=Michael |title=Professor Edward Hall |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/professor-edward-hall-9260740.html |access-date=15 May 2023 |work=The Independent |date=15 August 2001 |language=en}}</ref> His thesis was on the "development of an [[x-ray fluorescence]] [[spectrometer]] for the non-destructive analysis of archaeological material".<ref name="RLAHA">{{cite web |title=Research Laboratory for Archaeology and the History of Art |url=https://www.arch.ox.ac.uk/research-lab-archaeology-and-history-art |website=School of Archaeology |publisher=University of Oxford |access-date=15 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

==Career== 
In 1954, Hall became director of the newly founded [[Research Laboratory for Archaeology and the History of Art]] (RLAHA) at the [[University of Oxford]]. In 1969, he was elected a [[Fellow (Oxbridge)|fellow]] of [[Worcester College, Oxford]]. He was made Professor of Archaeological Sciences in 1975. On retirement from RLAHA in 1989, he was made [[emeritus professor]].<ref name="WWW" />

Hall was a member of the council of the [[International Institute for Conservation]] from 1971 to 199?, and served as its president from 1989 to 1992.<ref name="WWW" /> He was a [[trustee]] of the [[British Museum]] (1973–1995), [[National Gallery]] (1977–1984) and [[The Science Museum]] (1984–1992).<ref name=":0" /><ref name="WWW" /> He was also Prime Warden of the [[Worshipful Company of Goldsmiths|Goldsmiths Company]].<ref name=":0">{{Citation|last=Pollard|first=A. Mark|title=Hall, Edward T |date=2014|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-0465-2_347|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Global Archaeology|pages=3189–3191|editor-last=Smith|editor-first=Claire|place=New York, NY|publisher=Springer|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-0465-2_347|isbn=978-1-4419-0465-2|access-date=2022-01-04|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Other activities==
Hall was also a hot-air-balloon pilot and owner of [[Cameron Balloons|Cameron]] O-84 ''Flaming Pearl'' G-AYAJ 1970–1990. He was a member of the [[Air Squadron]].<ref name=":0">{{Citation|last=Pollard|first=A. Mark|title=Hall, Edward T |date=2014|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-0465-2_347|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Global Archaeology|pages=3189–3191|editor-last=Smith|editor-first=Claire|place=New York, NY|publisher=Springer|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-0465-2_347|isbn=978-1-4419-0465-2|access-date=2022-01-04|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In 1962, Hall co-developed, with his friend [[Robin Cavendish]], a wheelchair with a built-in respirator that allowed Cavendish, who was paralyzed from the neck down from [[polio]] and required a [[medical respirator]] to breathe, to leave the confinement of his bed. This chair became the model for future devices of its type,<ref>Renton, Alice; Renton, Tim (10 August 1994). [https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituary-robin-cavendish-1382697.html "Obituary: Robin Cavendish"]. ''[[The Independent]]''.</ref> with Cavendish eventually using a total of 10 different chairs.<ref name="HallObit">Oaksey, John (17 August 2001). [https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1337670/Professor-E-T-Teddy-Hall.html "Obituaries: Professor E T 'Teddy' Hall"]. ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]''.</ref> This part of Hall's life is shown in the 2017 film ''[[Breathe (2017 film)|Breathe]]''.

===Achievements===

{{more citations needed section|date=March 2017}}
He was influential in exposing the [[Piltdown Man]] fraud which led to his founding the [[Research Laboratory for Archaeology and the History of Art]], [[Oxford University]].<ref name="HallObit"/>
He founded Littlemore Scientific Engineering Company (ELSEC).
He helped to [[Radiocarbon 14 dating of the Shroud of Turin|date]] the [[Shroud of Turin]] to the period 1260–1390.<ref name="'Turin Nature">{{cite journal|last1=Damon|first1=P. E.|last2=Donahue|first2=D. J.|last3=Gore|first3=B. H.|last4=Hatheway|first4=A. L.|last5=Jull|first5=A. J. T.|last6=Linick|first6=T. W.|last7=Sercel|first7=P. J.|last8=Toolin|first8=L. J.|last9=Bronk|first9=C. R.|last10=Hall|first10=E. T.|last11=Hedges|first11=R. E. M.|last12=Housley|first12=R.|last13=Law|first13=I. A.|last14=Perry|first14=C.|last15=Bonani|first15=G.|last16=Trumbore|first16=S.|author16-link=Susan Trumbore |last17=Woelfli|first17=W.|last18=Ambers|first18=J. C.|last19=Bowman|first19=S. G. E.|last20=Leese|first20=M. N.|last21=Tite|first21=M. S.|title=Radiocarbon dating of the Shroud of Turin|journal=Nature|date=16 February 1989|volume=337|issue=6208|pages=611–615|doi=10.1038/337611a0|bibcode=1989Natur.337..611D |s2cid=27686437|url=https://cloudfront.escholarship.org/dist/prd/content/qt6x77r7m1/qt6x77r7m1.pdf?t=nusjjr}}</ref> 
He built the Littlemore Clock in the 1990s, which is the most accurate pendulum clock ever built.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Hall, E.T. |date=June 1996|journal=Horological Science|url=http://www.hsn161.com/HSN/hsn_article.php|title=The Littlemore Clock}}</ref>

==Personal life==
He married South African model Jennifer De La Harpe and had two sons Bill and Martin.<ref name=":0" />

==Honours==
In 1951, Hall was elected a [[Physical Society of London|Fellow of the Physical Society]] (FPhysS), a [[learned society]] for the physical sciences.<ref name="WWW" /> In 1984, he was elected an [[Honorary Fellow of the British Academy]] (Hon FBA), the United Kingdom's national academy for the humanities and the social sciences.<ref name="FBA">{{cite web |title=Professor Edward Hall FBA |url=https://www.thebritishacademy.ac.uk/fellows/edward-hall-FBA-hon/ |website=The British Academy |access-date=15 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref>
